Title: AI Writes 41% of Code. Only 29% of Devs Trust It. Review It Like a Senior Engineer - DEV Community
# AI Writes 41% of Code. Only 29% of Devs Trust It. Review It Like a Senior Engineer. 41% of all code produced globally is now AI-generated — and in some organizations AI authorship already sits at 90%. Only **29%** of developers trust the accuracy of the tools that write it, and **66%** report spending more time debugging AI output than expected. Treat AI code like code from a capable junior who is fast, confident, and occasionally hallucinating: verify behavior by **execution, not by reading**; treat tests as **evidence, not proof**; resolve every suggested dependency against the registry; and **never auto-merge**. Stack Overflow's 2025 survey (49,009 developers) shows a workforce that adopted AI universally and lost faith in it simultaneously:. * Trust in accuracy of AI answers fell **40% → 29%** in a single year. * Between **45% and 66%** name "almost right, but not quite" as their top frustration — the exact failure mode that turns a five-minute review into a forty-minute archaeology session. The new constraint is reviewing it.**. 2. **Run the code, don't read it.** Execute the happy path *and* the error path. **Timebox verification.** Reviewing a 400-line generated diff is not faster than writing 80 lines by hand. Point 1 and point 7 are doing the real work here — "does killing a mutant fail the suite" is the sharpest one-line test for whether your test suite is actually testing anything, and it would have caught something I hit directly: a change logged as "FIXED" in a diary entry, based on passing tests, that turned out on re-investigation to be a false positive — the tests passed because they weren't exercising the actual mechanism, not because the bug was gone. The METR number is worth sitting with longer than most people give it: forecast 24% faster, self-assessed 20% faster, measured 19% *slower* — three different numbers about the same work, and only one of them is real. Same lesson as your Tier 2 "never auto-merge, mechanical gates not honor system" point: the failure mode isn't dishonesty, it's confident measurement error, and only enforced verification catches it before it ships. If AI writes 41% of code, who tests the testers?

results.title: The AI Writes Code, But the Engineer Creates Value
results.content: # The AI Writes Code, But the Engineer Creates Value. featured image - The AI Writes Code, But the Engineer Creates Value. > “Hey, we have a new feature requirement, how fast you can deliver this?”. > “Why don’t you use AI, it should help you delivering the feature in not time.”. When I asked it to write a new script with a very clear objective, it was fantastic. In a matter of seconds, it gave me a solid code, it was a nice jump start. Then trouble started when I noticed a small, trivial bug and trying to fix it by talking to the AI was often more work than just fixing it myself. Frustrating at times, I felt as though I was correcting my new "helper" more often than it was saving me. But I kept experimenting, some of that was forced by new mandates at work and that's when my viewpoint started to change. I started realizing that I was expecting the GenAI to perform at least at the same level as I am implicitly. I was expecting a perfect, senior level expert who can just read my mind with couple of sentences as prompt. The real discussion of this article isn't about how fast AI writes code, but about how we, as engineers, create real value for our businesses in this new era. Real impact of GenAI is impacting all stages of the software development lifecycle (SDLC), not just code development. So, the use case we have for GenAI is to act as a product manager and brainstorming user stories and requirements. Can I use GenAI to "Jump Start" on the development of a new feature? If I need a Python script to read data from a CSV and call an API, I can write prompt explaining this, and a tool like Copilot will generate the initial code. With tools like copilot, I was just able to give it whole repository and ask the questions like, "What is the purpose of the UserService.cs file?" or "What type of database this solution utilizes?" It was able to provide me direct answers, acting as a powerful search engine and interpreter for the code itself.

Title: 🧠 How to Review AI-Generated Code Like a Senior Engineer - DEV Community
## DEV Community. Cover image for 🧠 How to Review AI-Generated Code Like a Senior Engineer. # 🧠 How to Review AI-Generated Code Like a Senior Engineer. AI can write code very fast. Tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and ChatGPT can generate functions, APIs, and even full features in seconds. The real challenge is knowing whether the code is safe to ship to production. Senior engineers don’t just read code. *Here’s a simple way experienced developers review AI-generated code.*. AI usually writes code for the happy path. Review whether the code handles:. Senior engineers assume inputs will break and design the code to handle it. AI-generated code often hides assumptions. 🔹 “The API always returns status 200”. 🔹 “The list will never be empty”. Before accepting the code, ask:. ✔ Where does this data come from? ✔ Can the database return unexpected results? AI sometimes produces code that looks clean but hides complexity. 🔹 Long functions doing too many things. If you can’t explain the code in a few seconds, it’s probably too complex. Many AI snippets have weak error handling. Silent failures are one of the biggest risks in AI-generated code. 🔹 Catching errors but ignoring them. 🔹 Returning default values when something breaks. Senior engineers prefer visible failures over hidden ones. AI does not always optimize code. AI can accidentally generate insecure code. Even if the code works, it may not fit your system design. Good code must fit the existing architecture, not just the feature. AI rarely produces strong tests. Testing is what turns working code into reliable code. But engineering value comes from judgment and review. A senior asks: “What could break in production?”. That mindset is what separates code generators from real engineers. results.title: How do you go from junior to staff engineer when AI writes the code? | CIO
results.content:
The path used to be well-known. As a newly hired junior software engineer, you were given an experienced mentor who would assign you simple tasks to learn the ropes. You’d write some code, ask plenty of questions, open a pull request, get feedback in code review, think about it and fix your code. Rinse and repeat that a few hundred times. The tasks became more complex; the feedback got shorter and along the way you’ve been building judgment, the thing that separates a senior engineer from a junior one.

Now AI writes most of the code. The loop looks different and the easy assumption is that it’s broken: fewer tasks for juniors to cut their teeth on, an agent fixing the code that another agent wrote, thinner path to judgment.

## Mentoring got easier, not harder [...] Opinion

Jul 14, 202610 mins

## AI might write the code now, but becoming a senior engineer is still about learning how to handle ambiguity and refusing to let bots think for you.

Happy Indian intern listening to mentor, consulting corporate teacher at shared office workplace in training center, discussing new professional skills, smiling. Business education, internship

Credit: fizkes / Shutterstock

A few weeks ago, a new hire at Aviator, fresh out of college, asked me a question I didn’t have a clean answer to. How do I become a senior engineer, or even a staff engineer? What should I learn, and how?

It’s a fair question and a harder one to answer than it was just a year ago. [...] When a junior gets stuck now, their first move usually isn’t to message a senior on Slack. It’s to ask the agent. This is also the case in code reviews. The purpose of code reviews was always knowledge sharing as much as it was a quality gate. What I see junior engineers do now is take the feedback and, without reading it closely, hand it straight to the agent to resolve. The part where they would have to understand how their work differed from what the senior expected disappears. It got passed from the reviewer to the agent, and the junior skipped the understanding.
